name: Isaac Newton
note: I keep Newton's synthesis of force and orbit beside the observations and geometry that made it possible.

name: Johannes Kepler
note: I remember Kepler's measured ellipses before Newton made the ellipses dynamical, and I keep Kepler's botanical observation in the golden-angle lineage.

name: Leonhard Euler
note: I give Euler the spiral, the notation, and a place where analysis feels almost musical.

name: Georges Lemaître
note: I put Lemaître's 1927 expanding-universe paper back beside the observations that followed.

name: Edwin Hubble
note: I credit Hubble's observations without letting the later naming erase Lemaître's derivation.

name: Max Planck
note: I remember Planck's reluctant quantum as a mathematical rescue with physical consequences.

name: Pierre-Simon Laplace
note: I follow Laplace from celestial mechanics into the moving sea.

name: Joseph Fourier
note: I let Fourier's rotating pieces rebuild heat, sound, and shape.

name: Claude-Louis Navier
note: I keep Navier's contribution to viscous flow in the equation's name.

name: George Gabriel Stokes
note: I place Stokes beside Navier in the continuum mechanics that carries both names.

name: Jean le Rond d'Alembert
note: I start the string's story with d'Alembert's equation and its traveling shapes.

name: Edward Lorenz
note: I show Lorenz's compact system as a weather model that opened a door into chaos.

name: James Clerk Maxwell
note: I pair Maxwell's field equations with the experiments and intuitions that made the synthesis possible.

name: Michael Faraday
note: I let Faraday's lines of force stand as more than a preface to Maxwell.

name: Fibonacci of Pisa
note: I name Fibonacci's book as a carrier of Indian and Arabic mathematics, not an origin story made in Europe.

name: Martin Vogel
note: I use Vogel's 1979 model to make the spacing argument visible in a sunflower-like disc.

name: Alan Turing
note: I read Turing's last paper as a bridge from reaction to form.

name: Alfred Lotka
note: I put Lotka's chemical and biological cycles beside Volterra's ecological equations.

name: Vito Volterra
note: I keep Volterra's predator-prey model grounded in a wider ecology of ideas.

name: Godfrey Harold Hardy
note: I let Hardy's algebra stand while his reported distance from biology stays a historical aside.

name: Wilhelm Weinberg
note: I give Weinberg's independent result equal type and credit his medical perspective.

name: Alan Hodgkin
note: I follow Hodgkin's measurements into the electrical language of a nerve.

name: Andrew Huxley
note: I place Huxley's gating model beside Hodgkin's experiments and the squid axon.

name: Erwin Schrödinger
note: I let Schrödinger's wave packet make probability feel spatial without hiding the formalism.

name: Emmy Noether
note: I put Noether's theorem at the center because symmetry and conservation deserve a center.

name: Ludwig Boltzmann
note: I hold the microstates and the arrow of time together in one logarithm.

name: Claude Shannon
note: I measure surprise in bits and let information become something countable.

name: Werner Heisenberg
note: I treat uncertainty as a structure of states, not a flaw in a measuring hand.

name: Pythagoras of Samos
note: I name Pythagoras with care, alongside Babylonian tablets and the Chinese gougu tradition.

name: Thomas Bayes
note: I keep Bayes's essay as the seed, not the whole publication history.

name: Richard Price
note: I restore Price as editor, publisher, and mathematical interlocutor.

name: Bernhard Riemann
note: I follow Riemann from analytic continuation to the still-open line of zeros.

name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
note: I keep Gauss's intrinsic curvature beside the theorem that grew after him.

name: Pierre Ossian Bonnet
note: I place Bonnet's boundary contribution in the theorem's full name.
